question: What does the Bible say about the Sabbath?
intro: The Sabbath is the seventh day, a day of rest that the Bible roots in God's own rest at creation, gives as a commandment to Israel, and speaks of again in the sayings of Jesus and in the letters to the churches. Christians read these texts in different ways when they ask whether the command binds those who follow Christ, which day they keep, and what the New Testament means by rest. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that the Sabbath begins with God: He rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy. In the Law it is commanded to Israel as the seventh day, a Sabbath to the LORD, to be remembered and kept holy, and the rest reaches to sons and daughters, servants, foreigners and animals alike, so that those who serve may rest as their masters do. The Law gives two grounds for it, God's rest at creation and the LORD's bringing His people out of slavery in Egypt, and calls it a permanent covenant and a sign between the LORD and the Israelites, for the generations to come. Every reading also takes Jesus to have spoken of the Sabbath to hearers who kept it, saying that it was made for man and that it is lawful to do good on it. The readings differ on whether and how the command binds those who follow Christ today, which day is meant, and what the New Testament means by "rest".

passages.quote: Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on that day He rested from all the work of creation that He had accomplished.
Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy.
nor the foreigner within your gates, so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do.
Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.
The Israelites must keep the Sabbath, celebrating it as a permanent covenant for the generations to come.
It is a sign between Me and the Israelites forever; for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed.
The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.

readings.label: The seventh day still kept: the Sabbath commandment stands for the people of God, and the day God blessed at creation is the day to keep
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the Sabbath to be older than Sinai, set apart by God at creation and written among the Ten Commandments, which they take Jesus to have upheld when He said He had not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. They read the Gospels and Acts as showing Jesus, the women who followed Him and Paul keeping the seventh day, read the prophets as bringing foreigners and all mankind to the Sabbath, and read no verse as moving the day or ending the command. Seventh-day Adventist, Seventh Day Baptist and other seventh-day churches keep the seventh day, Saturday, as their day of rest and worship. No tradition listed on this page holds this reading as a whole, though individual members and congregations within some of them do; among Baptists, the Seventh Day Baptist General Conference keeps the seventh day, and its Statement of Belief describes that day as sacred time, a gift of God to all people, dating from creation and upheld in the Ten Commandments.

passages.quote: all who keep the Sabbath without profaning it and who hold fast to My covenant-
passages.note: Foreigners who join themselves to the LORD are described as keeping the Sabbath and holding to His covenant.

passages.quote: From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me,” says the LORD.
passages.note: Read as placing the Sabbath in the age to come, for all mankind.

passages.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them. For I tell you truly, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished.
passages.note: Read as Jesus upholding the Law, the Ten Commandments among it.

passages.quote: Pray that your flight will not occur in the winter or on the Sabbath.
passages.note: Jesus speaks of the Sabbath as a day His hearers will still be keeping at a time yet to come.

passages.quote: As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath.
passages.note: Jesus' custom, named by Luke, was to be in the synagogue on the Sabbath.

passages.quote: And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.
passages.note: The women who followed Jesus rested on the Sabbath after His death, as the commandment says.

passages.quote: As was his custom, Paul went into the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
passages.note: Paul's custom, named by Luke, includes the Sabbath assembly.

passages.quote: There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
passages.note: Read as saying that Sabbath keeping continues for God's people, the Greek word being sabbatismos.

passages.quote: Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike.
passages.note: Paul reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, with Jews and Greeks.

passages.quote: if you call the Sabbath a delight, and the LORD's holy day honorable
passages.note: The Sabbath is called a delight and the LORD's holy day.

passages.quote: I also gave them My Sabbaths as a sign between us, so that they would know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them.
passages.note: The LORD gave Israel His Sabbaths as a sign between them and Him.

passages.quote: they entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down
passages.note: Paul and his company went into the synagogue on the Sabbath at Pisidian Antioch.

passages.quote: the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath
passages.note: The Son of Man is called Lord even of the Sabbath.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the "Sabbaths" of Colossians 2:16 to be the Sabbaths of the festal calendar, listed there with feasts and new moons, and not the weekly day written in the Ten Commandments, and they take Romans 14:5 to speak of days of fasting and feasting that Scripture does not command. They take Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2 to describe a meeting and a collection on the first day of the week and to command no change of the day, and Revelation 1:10 to leave open which day is the Lord's day. They take Hebrews 4:9 to say that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and the Greek word there to name keeping the Sabbath.

readings.label: The Sabbath fulfilled in Christ's rest: the weekly day pointed ahead, and the rest it pointed to is found in Christ and shared by those who believe
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Paul to speak of the Sabbath, with feasts and new moons, as a shadow of things to come whose body belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16-17), and take Hebrews to speak of a rest that believers enter now and finally. Catholic teaching, in its catechism, holds that Sunday fulfills the spiritual truth of the Jewish Sabbath and keeps the third commandment as a day of worship and rest, rooted in the Lord's resurrection and the apostolic age and bound by the Church's precept (Catechism 2174-2185); Eastern Orthodox teaching and worship keep Sunday as the day of resurrection and of the liturgy, within the whole year's cycle of feasts, and the Longer Catechism of Philaret, in treating the fourth commandment, says the Church keeps the first day of the week, the Day of the Resurrection, in the place of the seventh, with rest from worldly work on Sundays and greater holy days for worship and works of charity; Lutheran confessions hold that the commandment is kept in hearing God's word and that Sunday is kept by church order and not by divine command (Augsburg Confession XXVIII; Large Catechism, Third Commandment), and the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod's Brief Statement calls Sunday an ordinance of the Church under Christian liberty; Anabaptist readers speak of the rest that Christ gives and of all time as holy through him, and the 1995 Mennonite confession says the church celebrates a day of holy rest, commonly the first day of the week, and is called to live by Sabbath justice at all times, drawing on the Sabbath year and the Jubilee. John Calvin, a founder of the Reformed tradition (whose confessions state the next reading), takes the seventh day as a figure of spiritual rest whose ceremonial part ended with Christ; he says he does not cling so to the number seven as to bind the church to it, and rejects the view that the moral part remains in one day in seven, while keeping a set day for worship and good order (Institutes 2.8.28-34). Members of other traditions keep Sunday in ways close to this: Southern Baptists, in the Baptist Faith and Message (Article VIII), call the first day the Lord's Day, a Christian institution that commemorates the resurrection, with its activities left to each Christian's conscience, and the article does not use the word Sabbath; the Church of God (Cleveland) Practical Commitments call Sunday the Christian day of worship, commemorating the resurrection, and cite Colossians 2:16-17. The traditions named differ among themselves on whether any day of rest binds the conscience; what they share is the reading that the weekly day finds its fulfillment in Christ.

passages.quote: Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath.
passages.note: Paul tells the church not to be judged over a Sabbath, among other observances.

passages.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.
passages.note: The Sabbath, with the rest, a shadow whose body is Christ.

passages.quote: One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.
passages.note: Read as leaving the keeping of days to the conscience of each believer.

passages.quote: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.
passages.note: Rest given by Jesus to those who come to Him.

passages.quote: For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
passages.note: The Sabbath placed under the authority of the Son of Man.

passages.quote: For somewhere He has spoken about the seventh day in this manner: “And on the seventh day God rested from all His works.”
passages.note: Hebrews names the seventh day and God's rest at creation, and goes on to speak of the rest that believers enter.

passages.quote: Now we who have believed enter that rest.
passages.note: Believers enter God's rest now, by believing.

passages.quote: For whoever enters God's rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His.
passages.note: Read as the rest of God Himself, entered through faith in Christ.

passages.quote: There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
passages.note: A Sabbath rest is said to remain for the people of God.

passages.quote: Let us not neglect meeting together
passages.note: Believers are urged not to neglect meeting together.

passages.quote: You are observing special days and months and seasons and years!
passages.note: Paul's words to people observing special days, months, seasons and years.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Genesis 2:3 to say that God blessed the day and does not say that He commanded it of Adam's descendants, and take the permanent covenant of Exodus 31:16 to be given to the Israelites and to belong to the covenant at Sinai that Christ's coming fulfills. They take Matthew 5:17 to say that Jesus fulfills the Law ("to fulfill them", with "until everything is accomplished" in 5:18), the Sabbath included, and Isaiah 56:6 and 66:23 to be fulfilled in a gathering of the nations to the LORD in Christ. They take the first-day meetings of Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2 and the Lord's day of Revelation 1:10 to show where the church gathered and not to transfer the fourth commandment to Sunday, and Hebrews 4:9 to name the rest into which believers enter and not a day of the week to be kept.

readings.label: The Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath: the commandment stands, and the day of rest and worship now falls on the first day, the day of the resurrection
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the Sabbath to be a creation ordinance given before Sinai, and its commandment to belong to the moral law that Christ did not abolish, so that one day in seven is still set apart for rest and worship. They hold that the apostolic church met on the first day of the week, the day of Christ's resurrection, which Revelation calls the Lord's day, and that the Sabbath rhythm moved to that day under Christ (what is called Sabbatarianism, or the Christian Sabbath). The Westminster Standards, held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, state this at length, calling the first day the Christian Sabbath (Westminster Confession 21.7-8; Larger Catechism 115-121; Shorter Catechism 57-62). The Heidelberg Catechism (Question 103), held by the Christian Reformed Church, speaks of the day of rest and of the eternal Sabbath begun in this life, without the Westminster account of one day in seven; Reformed churches differ in how strictly the day is kept, and Calvin's Institutes, set beside the second reading, does not state this reading. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (chapter 22) states this strictly, as a positive-moral and perpetual commandment, and other Baptists keep the day less strictly. The Church of England's Second Book of Homilies, in its homily Of the Place and Time of Prayer, says Christians keep the first day, Sunday, as their Sabbath, their day of rest, and many Anglican members hold the reading in differing degrees of strictness. The United Methodist Church's Confession of Faith (Article XIV) says the Lord's Day is divinely ordained for worship and rest from unnecessary work, and does not use the word Sabbath; Wesleyan members hold the reading in differing degrees of strictness. Pentecostal and Charismatic congregations differ widely, some holding this reading and others the second.

passages.quote: if you call the Sabbath a delight, and the LORD's holy day honorable,
passages.note: The Sabbath as delight and as the LORD's holy day, spoken to God's people.

passages.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them. For I tell you truly, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished.
passages.note: Read as Jesus leaving the moral law, the fourth commandment among it, in force.

passages.quote: Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD.
passages.note: A holy Sabbath to the LORD before the Law was given at Sinai, read as showing the command older than the Law.

passages.quote: It was the first day of the week, and that very evening, while the disciples were together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them.
passages.note: Jesus meets the gathered disciples on the first day, the evening of the day the tomb was found empty.

passages.quote: On the first day of the week we came together to break bread.
passages.note: The church gathered to break bread on the first day.

passages.quote: On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income,
passages.note: A weekly first-day practice among the churches.

passages.quote: On the Lord's day I was in the Spirit,
passages.note: Read as the name of the first day, the Lord's day.

passages.quote: There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
passages.note: Read as a weekly Sabbath rest that remains for God's people until the final rest.

passages.quote: Eight days later, His disciples were once again inside
passages.note: Eight days after the first meeting the disciples are inside again and Jesus comes to them; read as their meeting on the next first day of the week.

passages.quote: who keeps the Sabbath without profaning it
passages.note: Blessed is the one who keeps the Sabbath without profaning it.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the Sabbaths of Colossians 2:16 to be the ceremonial Sabbaths of the festal calendar, named there with feasts and new moons, and not the weekly day that stood in the Ten Commandments before them, and they take Romans 14:5 and Galatians 4:10 to concern days and seasons that Scripture does not command, or that were kept as a way of earning standing before God. They take Mark 2:27 and Matthew 12:8 to show Jesus guarding the day's purpose and not ending it, and Hebrews 4:9 to say that a Sabbath rest remains, the weekly day being a foretaste of the final rest of Hebrews 4:10.

terms.note: The Hebrew name of the seventh day, from the verb that means to cease or to rest, which Genesis 2:2-3 uses of God. Jewish communities keep it from sundown on Friday to nightfall on Saturday, as a sign and commandment given to Israel; this page sets out how Christians read what the Law, the Prophets and the New Testament say of it.

The Greek phrase in Revelation 1:10. Christians differ over whether it names the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection, or the day of the Lord in a prophetic sense, and over whether it is a Sabbath.

The name given to the teaching, held among Reformed and other Christians, that the fourth commandment binds believers and that the Lord's day is the Christian Sabbath. Members of those traditions differ on how strictly the day is kept.
The Greek word in Hebrews 4:9, used nowhere else in the New Testament. Readers differ over whether it names the weekly day, the present rest of believers in Christ, or the final rest.

In the Greek of Luke 24:1, John 20:19 and Acts 20:7 the phrase is literally "one of the Sabbaths" (mia ton sabbaton in Luke and Acts, mia sabbaton in John), the idiom translated "the first day of the week"; 1 Corinthians 16:2 has the singular (kata mian sabbatou). The word sabbaton is also the one translated "Sabbath". Readers agree that the first day of the week is meant and differ over what the meetings and gifts on that day show.
The term, held among Reformed and other readers, for a command or pattern given at creation and so, in their reading, for all people and not for Israel alone.

The Catholic term for the church's rule that the faithful keep Sunday as a day of worship and of rest from work, which Catholic teaching sets on the church's authority and relates to the third commandment; the Catechism traces Sunday itself to the Lord's resurrection and the apostolic age.
A name for churches that keep the seventh day, Saturday, as their day of rest and worship.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2174-2188 (The Third Commandment: The Lord's Day)
further_reading.says: It teaches that Sunday is distinguished from the Sabbath and fulfills the spiritual truth of the Jewish Sabbath (2175), traces the Christian assembly to the beginning of the apostolic age (2178), and sets the Church's precept to attend Mass on Sundays and to avoid work that hinders worship (2180-2185).

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 536-539 and 548-553
further_reading.says: It teaches that the Church does not keep the Sabbath strictly but keeps the first day of the week, the Day of the Resurrection or Lord's Day, in the place of the seventh, and that on Sundays and greater holy days worldly work is set aside for worship and works of charity.

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article XXVIII (Of Ecclesiastical Power)
further_reading.says: It teaches that Scripture has abrogated the Sabbath, that the Church appointed the Lord's Day, and that no day is necessary for salvation or earns grace.

further_reading.title: Luther's Large Catechism, Part First (the Ten Commandments), Third Commandment, paragraphs 78-102
further_reading.says: It teaches that the literal seventh-day rest, in its gross sense, does not concern Christians, that Sunday is kept for good order and to hear God's Word, and that the day is holy where the Word is taught and heard.

further_reading.title: Luther's Small Catechism, Part First (the Ten Commandments), Third Commandment
further_reading.says: It gives the Third Commandment as sanctifying the holy day and explains it as not despising preaching and God's Word but holding it sacred and gladly hearing and learning it.

further_reading.title: A Brief Statement of the Doctrinal Position of the Missouri Synod (1932), Of Sunday (paragraph 41)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the New Testament has set aside the Old Covenant Sabbath and holds that God commands no particular day, and calls Sunday an ordinance of the Church under Christian liberty, not binding on the conscience.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 21 (Of Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day), sections 7 and 8
further_reading.says: Section 7 calls one day in seven a positive, moral and perpetual commandment, changed after the resurrection to the first day of the week, the Lord's day, which continues as the Christian Sabbath; section 8 describes keeping it by rest from worldly labor and by worship and works of necessity and mercy.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 115-121
further_reading.says: Question 116 teaches that the fourth commandment requires one whole day in seven, the seventh until Christ's resurrection and the first day of the week since, which is the Christian Sabbath or Lord's Day.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, questions 57-62
further_reading.says: Question 59 teaches that the first day of the week, since Christ's resurrection, is the Christian Sabbath, and question 60 teaches that it is kept by rest from ordinary work and by public and private worship, apart from works of necessity and mercy.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, question 103 (Lord's Day 38)
further_reading.says: It teaches that God wills the ministry of the gospel to be maintained and the day of rest diligently attended, that each believer rest from evil ways, and that in this way the eternal Sabbath begins in this life; it does not say that one day in seven stands as a commandment moved to the first day.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 2, chapter 8 (Exposition of the Moral Law), on the fourth commandment
further_reading.says: Calvin takes the seventh day as a figure of spiritual rest whose ceremonial part ended with Christ, holds that a set day for hearing the Word, the sacraments and public prayer remains needed for the church's order, and rejects the view that the moral part remains in the observance of one day in seven, saying he does not cling so to the number seven as to bind the church to it.

further_reading.title: Second Book of Homilies, Homily 8 (Of the Place and Time of Prayer), Part 1
further_reading.says: It teaches that the fourth commandment does not bind Christians to the ceremonies of the Jewish Sabbath, and that Christians keep the first day, Sunday, as their Sabbath, their day of rest. The page is an independent reproduction of the text, not a Church of England site, and the Homilies are commended as doctrine by Article XXXV and are not a confession.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church, Article XIV (The Lord's Day)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the Lord's Day is divinely ordained for private and public worship and for rest from unnecessary work, commemorates the Lord's resurrection and is an emblem of eternal rest; the article does not use the word Sabbath.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 22 (Of Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day), paragraphs 7 and 8
further_reading.says: Paragraph 7 calls the Sabbath a positive-moral and perpetual commandment binding all people in all ages, changed after Christ's resurrection to the first day of the week, the Lord's Day; paragraph 8 describes keeping it in public and private worship and duties of necessity and mercy.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article VIII (The Lord's Day)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the first day of the week is the Lord's Day, a Christian institution for regular observance that commemorates the resurrection, and that its activities should be commensurate with the Christian's conscience; the article does not use the word Sabbath.

further_reading.title: Statement of Belief, on the Sabbath
further_reading.says: It describes the seventh day of the week as sacred time, a gift of God to all people, dating from creation, affirmed in the Ten Commandments and reaffirmed in the teaching and example of Jesus and the apostles, to be observed as a day of rest, worship and celebration.

further_reading.title: Church of God Practical Commitments, Spiritual Example (the Lord's Day)
further_reading.says: It states that Sunday is the Christian day of worship, that as the Lord's Day it commemorates the resurrection of Christ, and that it is to be used for worship, fellowship, service, teaching and evangelism, citing Colossians 2:16-17.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 21 (Christian Stewardship)
further_reading.says: It teaches that through Jesus all time is holy, that the church celebrates a day of holy rest, commonly the first day of the week, and that it is called to live by Sabbath justice at all times, drawing on the Sabbath year and the Jubilee.

_why:
QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked: Gen 2:3 (full verse); Exod 20:8 (full); Exod 20:11 (second sentence); Exod 31:16 (full); Deut 5:14 (final clause from 'nor the foreigner'); Deut 5:15 (first sentence); Mark 2:27 (from 'The Sabbath was made', the server text opens with 'Then Jesus declared, ' and an opening curly quote, which I left out; the server has no closing mark); Matt 12:12 (second sentence; the closing curly quote omitted); Isa 56:6 (clause from 'all who keep', hyphen as the server has it); Isa 66:23 (full verse, curly quote kept); Matt 5:17 (first sentence); Matt 24:20 (full); Luke 4:16 (clause from 'As was His custom'); Luke 23:56 (last sentence); Acts 17:2 (full); Heb 4:9 (full); Col 2:16 (full); Col 2:17 (full); Rom 14:5 (full); Gal 4:10 (full); Matt 11:28 (full); Matt 12:8 (full; closing curly quote omitted); Heb 4:3 (first sentence); Heb 4:10 (full); Isa 58:13 (clause 'if you call the Sabbath a delight, and the LORD's holy day honorable,'); Luke 24:1 (full); John 20:19 (first sentence); Acts 20:7 (first sentence); 1 Cor 16:2 (clause to 'income,'); Rev 1:10 (clause to 'Spirit,'). All ticked.

ORDER: the readings follow the question's own steps: the command stands as given (the seventh day kept); it is fulfilled in Christ; it stands, moved to the first day (the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath). No historical dating is claimed, and the order is not a ranking. It differs from the order the owner's scope note listed (kept, Lord's Day, fulfilled).

THE TORAH FIRST: the agreed block holds the Torah's own terms (creation, the commandment, the two grounds, the covenant given to Israel, the household and foreigner and servant included) before any Christian reading begins, since all three readings accept what it says. I did not describe the Sabbath in the agreed block as a 'Jewish observance that the church replaced' or in any similar terms; the card gives Shabbat as a term, notes that Jewish communities keep it (a fact outside the Berean text, stated plainly in the terms block and open to cutting), and avoids placing Jewish keeping in a reading as a position to be answered. A rabbi reading should say whether the agreed block says enough about Exodus 31:13-17 (the Sabbath as a sign between the LORD and Israel, which I quote only through v16 because v13 and v17 were not fetched; I would add 31:17 if the reviewer judges the sign language central), and whether Leviticus 23:3 and Exodus 16 (the manna, the first Sabbath keeping) merit a place.

HELD_BY FOR THE FIRST READING: the brief says seventh-day traditions are not on the allowed list, so held_by is an empty array and the summary says 'some churches keep the seventh day'. If the build rejects an empty list, the owner should say what to do; I did not assign it to Baptist / free church although Seventh Day Baptists exist, because the whole tradition does not hold it. The summary says that members of the listed traditions do not hold it as a body.

HELD_BY FOR THE OTHERS: approximate. Second reading: the summary names what each tradition says and that they differ among themselves on whether a day of rest binds the conscience (Catholic: Sunday precept; Lutheran: Sunday by church order; Orthodox: the liturgy and the feast cycle; Anabaptist: gathering). Third reading: Reformed is the clearest; Baptist, Wesleyan and Anglican members differ in strictness; Pentecostal / Charismatic is listed with the caveat that many hold the second reading. Nothing names a person, a scholar or a leader.

PASSAGES: agreed 8; first reading 8; second 8; third 8. Matt 5:17 and Heb 4:9 appear in more than one reading because holders of each cite them first; each carries that reading's own note. Heb 4:9 appears in all three, with a different note each time, since all three lean on it.

WORDS: I checked summaries, answers and notes for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely' and found none outside quotes (Col 2:17 carries 'but' as the verse's own word). 'Alone' and 'just' were avoided. The second reading's summary uses 'and not by divine command' for the Lutheran position; that is the position's own contrast and not a verdict.

RELATED: themes are creation, covenant, law_wisdom and new_creation, all in /api/majorthemes. Card ids verified with /api/entity: sabbath, ten_commandments, rest, covenant, law (the card named 'instruction', id law). I did not include the card 'jesus' or the divine persons.

DIVINE PERSONS: 'God', 'the LORD', 'Christ', 'the Son of Man', 'Jesus' used as the verses use them. Matt 12:8 and Mark 2:28 are cited with 'the Son of Man' and nothing added.

LEFT OUT: (a) Exod 31:13 and 31:17 (the Sabbath as a sign between the LORD and Israel), Lev 23:3 and Exod 16:23-30 (the Sabbath before Sinai through the manna, which the third reading and a rabbi's seat would both want), Neh 13:15-22 and Jer 17:19-27 (Sabbath-breaking and the exile), Ezek 20:12-20. Space only; I recommend adding Exod 31:17 to the agreed block and Exod 16 to the third reading. (b) Jesus' Sabbath healings (Luke 13:10-17, John 5:1-18, John 9) and John 5:17 ('My Father is working until now'), and Mark 3:4: left out for count; they bear on how the Sabbath is kept more than on whether, and a reviewer may want one of them. Matt 12:12 and Mark 2:27 stand for them in the agreed block. (c) Acts 15 (the Jerusalem council and the Gentiles) and Acts 13:42-44: the second reading's holders cite Acts 15 for the absence of a Sabbath rule for the gentile churches; I did not fetch it, so it is not quoted. (d) The church fathers, the Sunday laws, 'blue laws' and political questions about Sunday rest: kept out, since they are not texts, and since the political side differs for the young African American believer's reading (for whom Sunday is also the church's day in the community, with its own history). The page keeps the line between the Bible's words and any state's rules. (e) Whether keeping the Sabbath bears on salvation: left to the faith-and-works card.

READERS: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Wesleyan, Baptist, Pentecostal: each is named in the reading it would expect, with its strongest verses; the Pentecostal seat may find the diversity note too brief. Secular scholar of religion: nothing in the card asserts the history of Sabbath practice (the dates of the Sunday custom are not given). Biblical-theology teacher: Heb 4 carries three senses and the terms block names them. Rabbi: Torah first, the agreed block, Shabbat as a Jewish term, no reading characterises Jewish keeping, and I used 'Law' for the Torah only as the Berean does. Young African American believer: Deut 5:14-15 puts rest for servants and the memory of slavery in the agreed block, where every reading finds it.

UNRESOLVED: (1) empty held_by in the first reading; (2) the Jewish keeping sentence in the Shabbat term; (3) whether 31:17 and Leviticus 23:3 should be added; (4) the Catholic and Orthodox summary sentences are condensed and should be read by those seats.
